new_statements.quote: § 58. Kürzung in der Komposition. Das germanische Betonungsgesetz, nach dem der Hauptakzent auf die erste Stammsilbe fällt, macht sich in zusammengesetzten Wörtern darin bemerkbar, daß das zweite, nebentonige Kompositionsglied vielfach geschwächt wird, so in: öbrmarxdl Obermarchtal, duidl (Opp.) Tiefental, hoedne Heidenheim, ladss Lonsee, khirbe Kirchweih, noxbr Nachbar (zu der Vollform noxbaur s. S. 81), hédse Handschuhe, wisfl wieviel, fodl Vorteil, fäsnad Fastnacht, medek Montag, däesdek Dienstag, mid Mittwoch, dösdek Donnerstag, foidek Feiertag (Vgl. Bopp. S. 79; Kauffmann §§ 101, 102.).
new_statements.translation: § 58. Shortening in compounds. The Germanic stress law, according to which the main accent falls on the first stem syllable, makes itself felt in compound words in that the second, secondarily stressed member of the compound is frequently weakened, e.g. öbrmarxdl 'Obermarchtal', duidl 'Tiefental', hoedne 'Heidenheim', ladss 'Lonsee', khirbe 'Kirchweih', noxbr 'Nachbar' (beside the full form noxbaur), hédse 'Handschuhe', wisfl 'wieviel', fodl 'Vorteil', fäsnad 'Fastnacht', medek 'Montag', däesdek 'Dienstag', mid 'Mittwoch', dösdek 'Donnerstag', foidek 'Feiertag' (cf. Bopp p. 79; Kauffmann §§ 101, 102).
new_statements.citation: Strohmaier, Otto. 1930. Die Laute und die Flexion des Schwäbischen in der Mundart des Oberamts Blaubeuren. Inaugural-Dissertation, Universität Tübingen. Nürtingen a.N.: N. Henzler.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word stress falls on the first syllable of the stem (root-initial, Germanic pattern); in compounds the first member carries main stress and the second, secondarily stressed member is reduced (Montag > medek). Inflectional/derivational prefixes ge-, be-, ver- are unstressed and in this dialect mostly non-syllabic (gmaxd 'gemacht', blegd 'belegt', frirnad 'verirrt', same page), so native words are in effect initial-stressed. Corroboration: Bopp 1890:45-46 (Münsingen) treats first-syllable stress as the norm from which only given names deviate; Hiller 2003 (snippet only) states Swabian has no contrastive stress, native stems have a single stressable vowel, and loanwords are adapted with weight-insensitive initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Second members of compounds are 'nebentonig' (secondary-stressed) and frequently phonetically weakened/shortened (Strohmaier §58); Kauffmann 1890 §39 Anm.2 adds that Swabian compound members differ only minimally in expiratory strength, without the NHG main/secondary cut distinction. Frey 1975 (snippet) distinguishes Hauptton, Nebenton, unbetont.
new_statements.exceptions: Given names (Bopp 1890 §19: mrai 'Marie', annamrai, and hypocoristics from non-initial parts: rika < Friedrike, sdofl < Christoph) may not have initial stress; griasgot/phiagot 'Grüss Gott/Behüt Gott' vary between initial and second-syllable stress with a pragmatic nuance (Bopp p.21); loanwords: Hiller 2003 reports initial stress replacing source-language non-initial stress, Wagner 1889 lists loans with pretonic syllables (abodek 'Apotheke', grogodil 'Krokodil').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement framed via the Germanic stress law as operative in the Blaubeuren (Oberamt Blaubeuren, Alb/Danube) local Swabian dialect; evidence drawn from compound reduction in citation forms and place names. Not a dedicated stress chapter; modern dedicated treatments (Frey 1975 §Betonung, Russ 1990, Caro Reina 2019 ch.7, Hiller 2003) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the local Swabian dialect of the Oberamt Blaubeuren (Swabian Alb / upper Danube, East-/Middle-Swabian), which falls under swab1242 (Glottolog has no separate code for it). Supporting older sources describe Münsingen (Bopp 1890) and Reutlingen (Wagner 1889) Swabian; Kügler 2005 and Frey 1975 describe Stuttgart urban Swabian; Hiller 2003 describes Swabian generally (author's native variety). All are swab1242.

new_statements.quote: p. 177: "Auch in der Stärkeabstufung der Silben eines Taktes ist der Unterschied zwischen starken und schwachen Silben in der Mundart ziemlich gross. Im zweiten Takt [də ist Auftakt] von də | šdô'desôs (Kurve 36) hat die Silbe šdô den Hauptton, sôs den Nebenton, de ist unbetont, šdô ist also Starksilbe, sôs mittelstark, de schwach." — p. 179: "Folgt auf die exspiratorisch starke Ictussilbe unmittelbar eine zweite, schwächer betonte Silbe, so hat erstere den Tiefton, letztere den Hochton, so in der Silbe -əd von se'ofəd, in der Silbe bə von dôbəguæə."
new_statements.translation: p. 177: "In the gradation of strength of the syllables within a speech-measure, too, the difference between strong and weak syllables is fairly large in the dialect. In the second measure [də is an upbeat] of də | šdô'desôs (curve 36) the syllable šdô carries the main stress, sôs the secondary stress, de is unstressed; šdô is thus a strong syllable, sôs medium-strong, de weak." — p. 179: "If the expiratorily strong ictus syllable is immediately followed by a second, more weakly stressed syllable, the former has the low tone, the latter the high tone, as in the syllable -əd of se'ofəd, in the syllable bə of dôbəguæə."
new_statements.citation: Wagner, Philipp. 1891. Der gegenwärtige Lautbestand des Schwäbischen in der Mundart von Reutlingen. Zweite Hälfte. Reutlingen: Programm des Gymnasiums (pp. 177-185 on accent/syllable division per Fischer 1895).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Strohmaier statement (main accent on the first stem syllable) but silent on placement itself; adds phonetic detail: three-degree prominence with secondary stress, low tone on the stressed syllable + high tone on the following one (as Kauffmann 1890 §38-40 and Fischer 1895 §10), syllable-cut correlates of stress, vowel reduction and loanwords with unstressed initial syllables. Identity note on the listed copy: the open_url (HathiTrust uc1.b5142912) is v.1 only — the 1889 first half, 98 images (HathiTrust catalog API enumcron v.1; HTRC EF pageCount 98; MARC 500 'Vol. [1].. 1889 (p. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for where word stress falls is stated anywhere in the second half. § 74 distinguishes expiratory (dynamic) from tonic (musical) accent, describes sentence-level intensity differences between speech measures (Sprechtakte), three degrees of strength within a measure (Hauptton / Nebenton / unbetont) and syllable cut (stark vs schwach geschnittener Accent: strongly cut in stressed syllables with short vowel, weakly cut with long vowel). § 75 says the stressed (an earlier reading) syllable carries the low tone and a following weaker syllable the high tone (phonograph measurements pp. 179-181). The stressed 'Ictussilbe' is presupposed throughout (stem stress as in German) but never located.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees within a speech measure: Hauptton, Nebenton, unbetont (p. 177, example də | šdô'desôs). Long vowels are two-peaked with a 'Nebengipfel' carrying the high tone / 'Nebenaccent' (pp. 178-179, 188-189).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 189: in unstressed position almost all vowels reduce to ə or e, with loanword examples whose first syllable is unstressed (cěnərâl 'General', abədêc 'Apotheke', šogəlâd 'Schokolade', fadsǝnêdlě 'fazzoletto') — implicit non-initial stress in loans, no rule given. p. 179 Anm.: natives keep strongly-cut accent in French pa-tin, mai-son. § 77: syllable boundary shifts when a compound is felt as such (mãě-šdî-fl, šniər-šdîfl).
new_statements.identity_note: Wagner 1891 describes the town dialect of Reutlingen (curves from a 15-year-old native speaker, p. 181); the catalog's Strohmaier statement is Oberamt Blaubeuren Swabian and Bopp's is Münsingen. The listed HathiTrust item uc1.b5142912 is the 1889 first half (v.1), not the 1891 second half cited; the second half was read from BSB bsb11527844.

sources.citation: Kauffmann, Friedrich. 1890. Geschichte der schwäbischen Mundart im Mittelalter und in der Neuzeit. Strassburg: Trübner (archive.org geschichtedersch00kaufuoft, scanned text).
sources.note: §§38-40 'Accentuirung' (pp.20-22) treat the nature of the accent only: an earlier reading syllables carry weakly-cut accent and low tone rising c. two tones to the following weak syllable; §39 Anm.2: in nominal compounds Swabian lacks the NHG main/secondary (strong-cut/weak-cut) distinction, both members differ only minimally in expiratory strength. Placement (stem syllable) is presupposed, not stated.
